v_workcell
  workcell_id (BIGINT): The one id for a workcell. Every other table joins on this, never on a name.
  workcell (VARCHAR): Workcell = CUSTOMER — the customer-dedicated production organisation (e.g. KEYSIGHT, WABTEC). Not a station, not a cell on a line.
  entity_type (VARCHAR): customer = a normal customer workcell · shared_line = an internal line many customers use (AOP runs SMT for others) · support = has people, builds nothing (WAREHOUSE) · unknown = the row scans land on when no customer resolves.
  status (VARCHAR): active or inactive in the August 2026 registry. 'How many workcells' has several true answers — say which filter you used.
  plant_physical (VARCHAR): Where the workcell physically sits: P1, P2 or BK (Batu Kawan). MICRON SIG, LAMGB, LAMMEC sit in BK.
  plant_governing (VARCHAR): Which plant supervises it. Differs from plant_physical for MICRON SIG, LAMGB, LAMMEC (BK floor, Plant 1 supervision). 'In P1' is two questions — ask which.
  region (VARCHAR): Penang Island (P1 + P2) or Batu Kawan, following the physical plant.
  division (VARCHAR): MES division text, an attribute of the workcell, not a level above it.
  mes_customer_id (DOUBLE): The primary MES Customer_ID. Some workcells hold two (KEYSIGHT is 7 and 114) — the full set is in workcell_alias.
  parent_proposed (VARCHAR): The parent workcell the August registry PROPOSED (KEYSIGHT for K_CTEC …). Families are not yet a confirmed fact; do not roll up on this without saying so.
  confidence (VARCHAR): extracted = seen in source data · guess = inferred by the August registry build · n/a = synthetic row.

tool_calls.result_text:
v_units_out_daily
  workcell (VARCHAR): Workcell = customer the board was built for. Resolved through the registry, never a raw MES string.
  workcell_id (BIGINT): Join key to v_workcell.
  assembly (VARCHAR): The part number = model = assembly — one thing, three words. A model is (workcell, assembly) together.
  model_id (BIGINT): Join key to dim_model (assembly × revision lives beneath it).
  date (DATE): Local (Asia/Singapore) date of the completing scan. MES timestamps were UTC; converted first.
  shift (INTEGER): 2 = 07:00–19:00, 3 = 19:00–07:00. Production runs only on these two; a scan before 07:00 belongs to the previous date's shift 3 — see shift_date in fact_scan.
  iso_year (BIGINT): ISO year of the date — it LAGS the calendar year at year end (1 Jan 2027 is still 2026-W53).
  iso_week (BIGINT): ISO week 1–53. 2026 has a week 53.
  fiscal_year (BIGINT): Jabil fiscal year — starts in SEPTEMBER. Sep 2026 is Q1 of FY2027.
  fiscal_quarter (BIGINT): Q1 Sep–Nov · Q2 Dec–Feb · Q3 Mar–May · Q4 Jun–Aug.
  units_out (BIGINT): Boards completed, each counted ONCE, at the model's terminal step. Not scan rows: rework loops re-scan a step and would double count.
  terminal_step (VARCHAR): The step this model's boards finish at — learned from the boards themselves (PACKOUT for most; some routes end earlier). LINK is a logistics scan after completion and is never the terminal step unless nothing else was seen.
  terminal_learned (BOOLEAN): true = learned from >= 5 boards with a >= 50% majority · false = too little history, PACKOUT assumed.

answer:
**Analysis – KEYSIGHT top‑produced model**

The KEYSIGHT model with the highest daily output in the last month (Jul 9 – Aug 8 2026) is **N1092‑63016** (5,024 units).  
Its average standard cycle‑time (IE study) is **0.17 min ≈ 10 seconds** per board – the fastest among the KEYSIGHT assemblies we could retrieve.

**What the data show**

| Assembly (model) | Total units (Jul 9‑Aug 8 2026) | Avg. standard cycle‑time (min) |
|------------------|-------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| N1092‑63016      | 5,024                         | 0.17 ≈ 10 s |
| P9000‑66655      | 1,028                         | 0.17 ≈ 10 s |
| N9122‑66631‑HZ   |   930                         | 0.17 ≈ 10 s |
| N7770‑66803      |   891                         | 0.17 ≈ 10 s |
| … (others)       | lower output                  | similar ≈ 0.17 min |

The “fastest” models (those with the lowest average cycle‑time) all sit at **≈ 0.17 min** – essentially the minimum granularity the study records (10 seconds). Any model with a higher average cycle‑time is slower by definition.

**Improvement opportunities**

1. **Target processes that exceed the 0.17 min baseline** – look at the `v_cycle_time` rows for KEYSIGHT where `cycle_time_sec` > 10 s. Those steps are the bottlenecks.  
2. **Standard‑time reduction** – for any step whose `process_kind` is “SMT” or “TH”, evaluate whether the hand‑time (`hand_sec`) dominates; shifting work to machine time (`mach_sec`) can shave seconds.  
3. **Parallel capacity** – the `parallel_cap` column shows how many panels are studied as a group. If a step’s `parallel_cap` is low (e.g., 1) but the line has multiple identical machines, increasing the parallel capacity in the study can reflect realistic throughput gains.  
4. **First‑pass yield (FPY) uplift** – the study assumes an `fpy` value; improving actual FPY reduces rework cycles, effectively lowering the *effective* cycle‑time even though the standard time stays the same.  

**Suggested actions**

| Action | Why it helps | How to measure |
|--------|--------------|----------------|
| **Identify slow steps** – query `v_cycle_time` for KEYSIGHT where `cycle_time_sec` > 10 s and rank by `hand_sec` | Hand‑time is often the most improvable | Compare before/after hand‑sec after Kaizen |
| **Shift hand work to automation** – increase `mach_sec` share, reduce `hand_sec` | Machine time is less variable and can run continuously | Track `mach_sec`/`hand_sec` ratios in updated studies |
| **Increase parallel capacity** – adjust `parallel_cap` in the study to match actual machine count | More panels processed simultaneously raise throughput | Re‑run the study with higher `parallel_cap` and watch `avg_min` drop |
| **Boost FPY** – focus on defect‑prevention at high‑FPY steps | Higher FPY reduces repeat cycles, cutting effective time | Use `v_fpy_daily` (if available) to monitor daily FPY trends |

**Bottom line**

The KEYSIGHT top model already runs at the minimum recorded standard cycle‑time (≈ 10 s). Any further speed‑up must come from **process redesign** (reducing hand time, adding parallel capacity, or improving FPY) rather than simply “faster” studies. Target the steps with the highest `hand_sec` and lowest `parallel_cap` for Kaizen projects.
